doc.title: Willie J. Humphrey and Willie E. Humphrey Interview, 1959-03-15
doc.interviewee: Willie J. Humphrey and Willie E. Humphrey

title: Brother Earl: his instruments, circus and minstrel shows
summary: Willie J. describes his younger brother Earl, who moved from bass to trombone, and his work on a circus, minstrel shows and with Chris Kelly.

story.theme_name: Medicine shows, minstrels, circuses and the black theater circuit
story.community_name: On the road with minstrel, carnival and tent shows

blocks.x: I was wondering, Will, if you have a couple minutes to talk yet about your brother Earl. I've never met him. I hope we'll get to talk to him someday. But in case we don't for a while, if you could. Was he older, younger than you? No, Earl's next to me. Just about two years younger.
You're the oldest. You haven't worked there in September.
How old would he be in September, Earl? He'd be 56, I'd say he was. Yeah.

Or 50. No, in September he'd be 57, because I'd be 59 at these times. So he'd be close by two years or less. Did he start right on the trombone? No, he started on his shell. And he, by granddaddy, should write bass parts for him, you know. But he was smaller. Yeah. And then he, when he got here, he started playing the bass. And he had a trombone. I still got the trombone over there. I put it in condition. Old York trombone. And he started, my granddaddy started teaching him the trombone. And first thing you know, he was out here playing. Yeah. And he was out here playing. Yeah. He still plays bass. Yeah. Yeah.
He still plays bass. Well, yeah, but I don't know.
He still plays bass. Somebody said they heard him over there in Virginia.

But they don't play bass. Yeah. He was playing. He was playing around. He stopped playing the trombone. He didn't have no instruments to practice on. So, he started playing around here at these different bands and he worked this Jitney business. He worked under one of these Jitneys down there a long time. It was the first real job I think was when my daddy took him off on the circus and he worked with me in California. And, uh, when he came back, well, he went on the circus. He worked with Salesforce too. He used to be on the corner. He'd been all up the counter. He traveled much more than my daddy on that counter. Then he, I believe my dad took him out on a minstrel show. What minstrel is that you're on, Papa? My dad's a minstrel man too, you know.
He's playing minstrel. He was on the minstrel.

What's the name of that minstrel he was on? Old Man Quine show. It wasn't a rabbit foot. What was the other one? Old Man Quine show. What's the other show? Rabbit was owned by Quine. They had the rabbit foot and they had another show. I just remember. I just remember. I just remember. Oh, it was on a show. It wasn't a rabbit foot. It's, uh, it's operated by the same people. Oh, I used to kid all the time about that show. I can't think of it. But anyhow, he traveled minstrel shows.
Several of them called Georgia. No, it wasn't Georgia Minstrel.

No, it wasn't that, no. No, they had a whole lot of musicians traveling in Georgia, but if you tell me they had a fine band, they did. I remember Georgia Minstrel. Yeah. John Porter was in there, and I think, and, uh, Charlie McCurdy, and, uh, David Jones, he was quite young. He made all of that. No, after he traveled around, he worked with Chris Kelly around here a long time, and he played those jitney dances. That's about all I knew he played with. Yeah, well that was. On the roof over the minor. That's right, he played on the roof over the minor. That's right, he sure did.
